text: Name the chords you want: "make the chords Am F C G", "i–VI–III–VII" or "Fm Db Ab Eb", and Keys plays exactly those, voiced for the style, with the bass and melody following.
why: Producers often know the progression in their head, or took it from a song they love (the owner's free pass). Today named chords are ignored and you get random ones on a new track. It's the fastest way to "make the song in my head" without singing.

text: "Another one, but keep the kick and clap": re-roll only some drum sounds and lock the rest (keep the kick, new hats; keep the groove, new percussion).
why: A melodic-house producer usually likes the kick/clap pocket and wants fresh hats or percussion. Today "another one" rolls the whole kit (78-98% of hits kept in my runs, but the producer can't choose which ones), so a good kick pattern gets lost to a better shaker.

text: After a sung take, show the sung pitch line faintly behind the notes in the editor, and mark the notes that were moved to the key, so the singer can drag a note back to what they sang.
why: The owner's top complaint is that sung parts don't keep his notes. Even with UX-10/UX-14, key-snapping and quantizing will move some notes (40% of the fixture's notes moved in F minor). Seeing what was heard against what was kept builds trust, and fixing a note becomes one drag.
